sub: Named after “the Striking Calamity” (al-qāriʿah), its first word
theme: The Day of Resurrection strikes hearts with terror. People scatter like moths, mountains float like wool, and each person’s fate depends on whether his scales are heavy or light.
story: Revealed in Makkah, with no dispute about that, and among the earliest surahs. Its whole subject is the Resurrection and the Hereafter.
It opens by alarming the listener: a name, then a question, then a second question. Only then does it show the scene, in two short pictures of people and mountains.
Then come the scales. Whoever’s good deeds outweigh his bad lives a life that pleases him. Whoever’s scales are light falls into a pit of blazing Fire.

sections.title: The Day that strikes
sections.meaning: Al-Qāriʿah, the Striking Calamity. What is it? And what will make you know what it is? It is the Day people are like scattered moths, and the mountains like fluffed-up wool.
points: The Striking Calamity: what is it? What will tell you?
sections.matters: The repeated question builds dread before any answer comes. Then two pictures show everything reduced: people, who can think, lose all direction, and mountains, the hardest things on earth, blow away.
sections.story: No specific incident. Al-Qāriʿah is one of the names of the Day of Judgement, like Al-Ḥāqqah.
explained: Al-qāriʿah is the one that knocks hard: a name of the Day of Resurrection, because its terrors strike the heart. The name is said, then asked about, then asked about again, so it feels enormous before anything is described.

People will be like al-farāsh al-mabthūth: scattered moths, or swarming locusts, crashing into one another with no idea where to go. The solid mountains become al-ʿihn al-manfūsh, carded wool the faintest wind carries off, until nothing of them is left to see.
teaches: Take the Day of Judgement as seriously as the Quran does.
On that Day even people of intelligence will be lost and confused.
Nothing that looks solid in this world will last.
Prepare now for a Day of total confusion.
sections.hook: Al-qāriʿah is said three times in ayat 1–3. Ayat 4 and 5 are a pair: people ka- (like) moths, mountains ka- (like) wool, ending al-mabthūth and al-manfūsh.

sections.title: Heavy scales, light scales
sections.meaning: Whoever’s scales are heavy lives a life that pleases him. Whoever’s scales are light has Hāwiyah, the Pit, as his “mother”. And what will make you know what it is? A Fire, intensely hot.
points: Light scales: his home is the Pit
What is it? A blazing Fire
sections.matters: Everything comes down to the weight of deeds. Deeds are weighed, not counted, so sincerity matters: a few deeds done with true faith can outweigh many done carelessly.
sections.story: No specific incident. Once the terrifying scene has passed, the scales are set up and people split into two groups: the happy and the wretched.
explained: Mawāzīn are the scales. If good deeds outweigh bad, a person is in ʿīshah rāḍiyah, a life he is fully pleased with, in Paradise. If bad deeds outweigh good, his umm, his “mother”, is Hāwiyah: the Fire is the home he returns to and stays with, or he falls into it head first.

Hāwiyah is a name of Hell, a pit whose bottom can’t be reached. The question comes again, “What will make you know what it is?”, and the answer is short: nārun ḥāmiyah, a Fire at the peak of its heat, seventy times hotter than fire in this world.
teaches: Deeds are weighed, not counted: sincerity adds weight.
Keep adding good deeds so your scale is heavy.
Paradise is a life you will be fully content with.
Seek refuge in Allah from the Fire.
sections.hook: Ayat 6 and 8 mirror: fa-ammā man thaqulat mawāzīnuh, then wa-ammā man khaffat mawāzīnuh. Wa mā adrāka returns in ayah 10, echoing ayah 3.

groups.text: The Striking Calamity! What is it? And what will make you understand what it is?
People scatter like moths, and mountains become like fluffed-up wool.
Whoever’s good deeds weigh heavy will live a life that pleases him.
Whoever’s scales are light will have the Pit as his home.
And what is it? A Fire, blazing hot.

1.explain: Al-qāriʿah: the one that knocks hard. A name of the Day of Resurrection, because its terrors strike hearts with fear.

2.explain: Mā al-qāriʿah: what is it? The question is not asking for information; it makes the Day feel enormous.

3.explain: Wa mā adrāka: and what will make you know? A second question adds to the dread before any answer comes.

4.explain: Al-farāsh al-mabthūth: scattered moths, or swarming locusts. People crash into one another in confusion, going this way and that, until they are called to account.

5.explain: Al-ʿihn al-manfūsh: carded wool. The hard, solid mountains become so light that the faintest wind carries them, until they are level with the ground.

6.explain: Thaqulat mawāzīnuh: his scales are heavy, meaning his good deeds outweigh his bad deeds.

7.explain: ʿĪshah rāḍiyah: a life that pleases him fully, in Paradise.

8.explain: Khaffat mawāzīnuh: his scales are light, meaning his bad deeds outweigh his good, with nothing to balance them.

9.explain: Fa-ummuhu hāwiyah: his “mother” is the Pit. Either the Fire is his home, clinging to him like a mother, or he falls into it head first.

10.explain: Mā hiyah: what is it? Hāwiyah is made to feel enormous again. The final h is added for the pause.

11.explain: Nārun ḥāmiyah: a Fire intensely hot, at the peak of its heat, seventy times hotter than the fire of this world.
